name: Dewatermark.ai
tagline: Upload an image, let a model detect and erase the watermark, download the clean version.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The hard part of this product was solved in public years ago: LaMa, Stable Diffusion inpainting, and the whole lineage of open inpainting tools do exactly this job, and IOPaint already wraps them in a browser UI. A coding agent can stand up a local version in one sitting: drop an image, brush over the watermark, get a clean fill, download it. What you are actually paying Dewatermark for is the automatic detection step, so you never have to brush anything, plus GPU inference you do not have to own. Quality on flat backgrounds is near identical; quality on busy textures depends more on the model weights than on who wrapped them. Also worth saying out loud: most of the images people feed tools like this are not theirs, and your local build will happily remove your own watermarks too.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you paint a mask over a watermark and an inpainting model fills the region, with batch export.
requirements: about 2 GB of disk for model weights
a GPU if you want it fast, CPU works but is slow
whatYouLose: Automatic watermark detection, you will be brushing masks by hand
Hosted GPU inference, so CPU runs take seconds to minutes per image
A mobile friendly flow you can use from a phone
Tuned behavior on the specific repeating stock-photo watermarks they have clearly optimized for
Any kind of batch pipeline or API unless you build it
moatNotes: The detection model and the one-click flow are the product. The erasing itself is commodity open weights.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because brushing a mask is friction, and a tool that guesses the watermark region correctly on the first try feels like magic compared to a canvas and a brush size slider. Paying also means not installing Python, not downloading weights, and not discovering that CPU inpainting on a 4000px image takes two minutes. For someone who does this twice a year, a few dollars beats an afternoon. For someone doing it daily, the local build pays for itself fast.
notes: The erase is free and open; the convenience is the invoice.
prompt:
Build a local watermark removal tool. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry, everything runs on my machine.

Stack, do not deviate:
- Python 3.11 with FastAPI and uvicorn for the backend
- simple-lama-inpainting (LaMa) as the inpainting model, downloaded on first run and cached in ./models
- Pillow and NumPy for image handling
- Frontend is a single static index.html with vanilla JS and a canvas, no build step, no npm

In scope:
- Drag and drop or file picker for PNG, JPG, WEBP, single or multiple files
- Show the image on a canvas at fit-to-window scale, keep full resolution in memory
- Brush tool to paint a white mask over the watermark, with brush size slider, eraser, undo stack of at least 20 steps, and a clear-mask button
- A rectangle select mode as a faster alternative to brushing for boxy watermarks
- POST /api/inpaint takes the original image plus the mask PNG, upscales the mask to original resolution, runs LaMa, returns the result
- Show before and after with a drag slider, plus a download button that preserves original dimensions and format
- Batch mode: apply the same mask to every queued image when they share dimensions, write results to ./out
- Show elapsed inference time so it is obvious when the CPU is the bottleneck

Out of scope, do not build:
- Automatic watermark detection, user paints the mask
- Any login, payment, usage limit, or analytics
- Any hosted API call, the model must run locally

Deliverables: main.py, static/index.html, requirements.txt, and a README with exact run commands and a note that first launch downloads model weights. Any config goes in .env read via os.environ, no secrets hardcoded. Add a one-line notice in the UI reminding the user that removing watermarks from work they do not own is on them.
